cur:catacombs-bedoin-fragment-british-mu.summary: On the far left Christ raises the son of a widow; beside him stands a figure between two saints, perhaps the deceased; then Christ multiplies the loaves, followed by Moses at the altar and Moses receiving the tablets of the Law. Old and New Testament are again set side by side.
facts: The fragment was found at Bédoin (Vaucluse) and belongs to the British Museum (1993,0406.1).
It was photographed while on loan to the 'Eye to Eye with the Romans' exhibition at the Gallo-Roman Museum, Tongeren, in 2021.

cur:catacombs-met-bowl-base-miracle-scen.summary: A central figure is surrounded by a ring of small gold scenes of miracles, arranged around the circular base of a vessel. Such gold-glass bases, decorated with biblical scenes, were treasured in life and set at graves in death.
facts: The Metropolitan Museum titles it 'Bowl Base with Miracle Scenes' and releases its image under CC0.
cur:catacombs-met-bowl-base-miracle-scen.notes: The individual miracle scenes and the central figure could not be identified from the available photograph; date approximate.

cur:monumental-san-calling-peter-andrew.summary: Two fishermen in a boat haul a net heavy with fish from the blue water while Christ, standing on the shore with a disciple, stretches out his hand to call them. The scene, often read as the calling of Peter and Andrew (and sometimes as the miraculous draught of fishes), shows Christ summoning his first disciples to become 'fishers of men'.
facts: The thirteen scenes of the north wall show Christ's miracles and teaching; in all of them he appears young and beardless, robed in imperial purple.
The scenes were not arranged in biblical order but are thought to follow the Gospel readings of the Lenten liturgy in Theodoric's palace church.

princeton:13151.summary: Only part of a face survives on this broken marble slab: a long straight nose, the line of a moustache, the mouth and the start of a beard, carved in shallow relief beside broad roughened areas. Princeton identifies it as an icon of Christ from the decoration of a four-apsed (tetraconch) church. Even as a fragment it is an early witness to the bearded, frontal image of Christ in the churches of Byzantine Syria.
facts: It was excavated by the Princeton-led expedition to Antioch-on-the-Orontes (1931–1939) at Seleucia, Antioch's port, and has been in the museum since 1939.
It was published by Richard Stillwell in 'Antioch-on-the-Orontes III: The Excavations 1937–1939' (1941), pl. 25, no. 460.
princeton:13151.notes: Identification rests on the museum's title; the surviving features are consistent with a bearded Christ but are fragmentary. Museum display date ca. 490–550. Scripture omitted.
